568.title: The month of Jeth
568.hook: in Jeth, join with the One before whom all bow (Barah Maha, ang 134)
568.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Jeth, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Jeth stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and in the summer heat, especially around the remembrance of Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Sikhs set up chhabeel stalls serving cold sweetened water to passersby.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakh: the harvest month, when longing points to what's missing. The harvest is in. Now the heat arrives, and the third month asks for something new.

By late morning the roads shimmer. Shops pull their shutters halfway down. This is Jeth, roughly May into June in Punjab, hot in a way that changes how people live. Anyone who can stays indoors through the afternoon, and the dust storms called aandhi can turn the sky brown. In that heat, even the proudest person slows down and looks for shade. Nobody walks tall at two in the afternoon in Jeth. And this is the month Guru Arjan chooses to talk about the One before whom every head goes down.
screen: `MAY INTO JUNE: THE ROADS SHIMMER.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS FOR SHADE.` → `EVERY HEAD GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Jeth stanza is on ang 134. It opens, in paraphrase: in Jeth, the longing is to be joined with the Lord, before whom everyone bows. Not some. Everyone. Kings and laborers, the clever and the simple, the powerful and the poor are all, sooner or later, lowered. The heat makes that easy to picture. Then an image of safety: one who holds the hem of the beloved Friend's robe can't be bound by anyone. It's an old picture, a child or a petitioner clinging to the edge of someone's garment, and protected. Then a picture of riches. The Name of the One is like rubies and pearls, and no thief can break in to steal them. In an old village, valuables could be stolen and houses broken into. Here is wealth no one can carry off. The stanza goes on: the One does whatever pleases the One, and creatures act accordingly; those the One makes His own are called blessed. And it ends: in Jeth, the joyful Lord is met by the one whose forehead carries that good fortune. Put the pieces together: bowing, holding on, a treasure that can't be stolen. Jeth's lesson isn't about pushing through the heat on your own strength. It's about lowering yourself and holding on. In a month when everything outside presses down, the stanza turns the pressure into a bow.
screen: `BEFORE WHOM EVERYONE BOWS.` · `HOLDING THE HEM OF THE FRIEND.` · `JEWELS NO THIEF CAN STEAL.` · `THE PRESSURE BECOMES A BOW.` · then, large: `JETH: BOW.`

segments.voice: Notice one pressure on you right now, tiredness, a deadline, real heat, a weight in the chest, and don't push against it. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, lower your head slowly, as if bowing to something greater than the pressure; stay low a breath or two, picturing the edge of a friend's robe in your hand, then rise. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.
Jeth. The month of hard heat, when Guru Arjan longs to be joined with the One before whom everyone bows, whose Name is a treasure no thief can steal.
Your line: jeth: bow. Some treasures are out of every thief's reach. That's five hundred sixty-eight.

569.title: The month of Asarh
569.hook: in Asarh the heat burns those who don't have the Lord near (Barah Maha, ang 134)
569.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Asarh, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Asarh stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, as the summer heat waits on the rains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeth, and its line: jeth: bow, a pressure turned into a bow. The heat isn't over. In Asarh it presses on, and the rains still haven't come.

June into July. The fields are cracked. The canals run low. Everyone keeps looking at the sky, waiting for the monsoon, and every day the clouds gather and don't break. People sleep on rooftops for a breath of air. The heat of Asarh wears on tempers, patience and sleep. Some people get short and sharp in weather like that. Maybe you're one of them. Guru Arjan looked at that burning month and saw something in it: the same heat doesn't land the same way on everyone.
screen: `CRACKED FIELDS, WAITING FOR RAIN.` → `SLEEPING ON ROOFTOPS.` → `THE SAME HEAT, NOT THE SAME FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: The Asarh stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Asarh, the heat scorches those whose Husband Lord isn't near them. They've left the One who is the life of the world, and put their hope in mortal people. Caught up in duality, in what is second, they're ruined, and death's noose is around their neck. As they sow, so they reap; what is written comes to pass. A whole life passes like a night: the night slips by, she regrets it, and she leaves without hope. Then the turn: Asarh is pleasant for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell. Same month, same heat. For one person it's a furnace; for another it's bearable, even pleasant. The difference isn't the weather. It's what's near. Slow down on one line: they put their hope in mortal people. Guru Arjan isn't saying don't rely on anyone. Sikh life is built on sangat, community. The problem is resting your whole hope on people who are themselves passing, who get tired and short in the heat too. When everything you lean on is also burning, there's nowhere cool to stand. The sowing and reaping line is a farmer's knowledge, in a month of waiting for rain: a harvest is the fruit of what was planted, and a life gives back what was sown. And the cool center stays the same: the Lord's feet dwelling in the heart. Keep the One near, and the heat changes.

segments.voice: Breathe slowly, imagining cool air on the out-breath, and think of someone running hot right now: stressed, short-tempered, overwhelmed. Without judging their heat, picture bringing them something cool, a glass of water, a calm word, ten minutes of help, or simply not adding to their pressure. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
Asarh. The heat before the rains: it scorches those far from the One, and is pleasant for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell.

570.title: The month of Sawan
570.hook: in Sawan the bride blossoms who loves His lotus feet (Barah Maha, ang 134)
570.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Sawan, many gurdwaras read the Sawan stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, while in Punjab the monsoon month is also marked by the folk festival of Teeyan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asarh: the same heat scorches or soothes, depending on what's near. After all that waiting, the clouds finally break.

Anyone who has lived through a North Indian summer remembers the first real rain. The smell comes before the drops: wet dust, sharp and sweet. Then the sky opens. Kids run into the street. Peacocks call from the fields. Within days, cracked brown ground turns green, swings go up in the trees of Punjabi villages, and girls and women gather to sing the songs of Teeyan. Sawan, July into August, is when the whole land seems to exhale. And in the folk barah maha, it's the month the waiting bride feels most alive, and most alone.
screen: `THE SMELL OF THE FIRST RAIN.` → `BROWN GROUND TURNS GREEN.` → `SWINGS IN THE TREES.`

segments.voice: The Sawan stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Sawan, the bride blossoms who loves the lotus feet of the Lord. Sarsee: she blossoms, she flourishes, the way the land does when the rain comes. Her mind and body are dyed in true love; the Name alone is her support. Then a contrast: the pleasures of poison, as the stanza calls them, are false, and everything seen of them turns to ash. Then the rain image, turned inside out. The drop of the Lord's nectar is beautiful, and those who meet the holy ones drink it in. The forests and meadows are refreshed by the One, the all-powerful, the infinite. Look at what Guru Arjan does with the monsoon. In the folk songs, the rain makes the separated woman ache: everyone else is together under the swings. Here, the rain is what happens to the soul that loves the One. She's the land; the love is the rain. And she doesn't just survive the season; she blossoms. Sawan is the first month in this Barah Maha that sounds almost like arrival. It isn't all joy; the warning about false pleasures turning to ash is still there. But the main image is green. After Jeth and Asarh, where the lesson was bowing and keeping the One near, Sawan shows what that nearness looks like when it rains. The lotus feet, charan kamal, is an old and tender image in Indian devotion, and Gurbani uses it often: the Beloved's feet, soft as a lotus, are where the devotee comes to rest.
screen: `SARSEE: SHE BLOSSOMS.` · `FALSE PLEASURES TURN TO ASH.` · `A DROP OF THE LORD'S NECTAR.` · `THE SOUL IS THE LAND; LOVE IS THE RAIN.` · then, large: `SAWAN: BLOSSOM.`

segments.voice: Watch rain at a window if it's falling, or pour a glass of water slowly and watch it fill, or simply picture the first drops darkening dry dust. Breathe slowly, and let the picture soften something in you that's been dry, watered without needing to understand it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each slow breath.
Sawan. The monsoon month: the bride who loves the Lord's lotus feet blossoms, like land under the rain, and drinks the drop of nectar.

571.title: The month of Bhadon
571.hook: in Bhadon she is lost in doubt, attached to what is second (Barah Maha, ang 134)
571.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Bhadon, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Bhadon stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, with its warning against bharam and its promise of the One's sanctuary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sawan: the soul is the land, and love is the rain. The rains go on, but the air turns heavy, and the green starts to feel close and confusing.

The rain has stopped being a relief. Clothes won't dry. Mosquitoes are everywhere. This is Bhadon, roughly August into September, the sticky end of the monsoon. The air is so thick it's hard to think, and the paths that were clear in spring are overgrown and muddy. It's easy to lose your way in a field in Bhadon. Guru Arjan says the soul can lose its way too, in a fog a lot like that weather, and he has a word for it.
screen: `AUGUST INTO SEPTEMBER: STICKY AIR.` → `PATHS OVERGROWN AND MUDDY.` → `A WORD FOR THE FOG.`

segments.voice: The word is bharam. The Bhadon stanza on ang 134 opens, in paraphrase: in Bhadon, she has lost her way in bharam, attached to the second. Bharam is often translated doubt, but that can mislead. In Gurbani it isn't the honest question a curious person asks. It's closer to delusion, a mind going round in circles in the fog. And doojaa, the second, is Gurbani's word for duality: loving something else in place of the One. Then the stanza gets hard. She may adorn herself a hundred thousand ways; it accomplishes nothing. On the day the body perishes, people will speak of it as a ghost. Death's messengers seize her and lead her away, and tell no one their secret. Those she was attached to every day leave her standing in a moment. She wrings her hands; her body writhes; the black hair has turned white. As she sows, so she reaps: karma is the field. It's a vivid, uncomfortable picture, and meant to be: a life spent in the fog, decorated outside, lost inside, waking only when it's too late to plant anything new. But the stanza doesn't end there. Nanak seeks the One's sanctuary, it says, and the One gives the boat of His feet. Those protected by the Guru aren't thrown into hell in Bhadon. So the fog has an exit: not thinking harder, not more adornment, but taking refuge. The boat is the same image as the Guru's boat in the Asa di Var: what carries you across when you can't find the path on foot.

Find one place where your mind keeps circling without getting anywhere, a worry you replay, a choice you keep avoiding, and name it plainly in one sentence, since naming it can thin the fog a little. Then picture stepping into a boat that carries you across without having to figure it all out first, and if you pray, say Waheguru.
Bhadon. The heavy end of the rains, when the soul is lost in bharam, attached to the second, until it takes refuge in the boat of the One's feet.

572.title: The month of Assu
572.hook: in Assu love wells up: how can I meet the Lord (Barah Maha, ang 135)
572.howItsDone: On the Sangrand that begins Assu, gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Assu stanza from the Barah Maha in Raag Majh, often with a short talk on its meaning for the month ahead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhadon: bharam, a mind lost in fog, and the boat of the One's feet. Today the rains end, and something in the bride starts to move.

By Assu, roughly mid-September to mid-October in Punjab, the monsoon has usually blown itself out. The mud dries, the nights cool, and the sky goes a hard, clear blue, the kind where you can suddenly see far hills that were hidden all summer. Doubt is a lot like the rainy season: while it lasts, you can't see past the next puddle. Then one morning the air clears, and what's left isn't certainty. It's wanting. You can see where you'd like to go, with no idea how to get there. That's exactly where Guru Arjan's Assu stanza begins.
screen: `ASSU: THE RAINS END, THE SKY CLEARS.` → `DOUBT GIVES WAY TO WANTING.` → `BUT HOW DO I GET THERE?`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: in Assu, love wells up. How can I go and meet the Lord? In Gurmukhi it begins asun prem umaahrraa. Prem is love. Umaahrraa is eagerness, a surge that rises on its own. Then the question that gives today its line: kiau milee-ai, how can I meet? Mind and body, the stanza says, are thirsty for a sight of the Beloved. And the bride does something very human. She calls out: O mother, will someone come and bring me to Him? The Barah Maha doesn't scold her for asking. In the Sikh reading, the question is the first step. Bhadon was confusion, attached to second things. Assu is the same person, now pointed in one direction, even without knowing the road. Then the stanza answers, gently. The saints are the helpers of love, and she falls at their feet. In Sikh life that points to the sangat, the company of people also on the way, and to the Guru's word they sing together. Without the Lord, the stanza asks, how can there be peace? There's no other place to go. It closes on grace: in Assu, those live in peace on whom the Lord shows mercy. So the answer to how isn't a technique. It's company, and longing, and a door opened from the other side. The not-knowing is allowed.

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow and ask, honestly, what you long for underneath the to-do list: peace, closeness, forgiveness, a sense of being found. If you pray, carry the stanza's own question on the breath, kiau milee-ai, how can I meet You; if you don't, just let the longing be there, without fixing or explaining it. Breathe in the wanting, and breathe out the hurry.
Assu. In Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, Assu is when love wells up and asks how to meet, and the stanza answers: through the holy company, and by mercy.

573.title: The month of Katak
573.hook: in Katak we reap what we did; blame no one else (Barah Maha, ang 135)
573.howItsDone: On the Sangrand of Katak, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Katak stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; it is heard as a call to take responsibility for their deeds while trusting in the Guru's grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Assu: love wells up and asks how to meet, and mercy answers. Today the Barah Maha turns from longing to honesty.

A dent appears on the family car. Nobody did it. Not the kids, not the spouse; the neighbor's teenager is the obvious suspect, and the shopping cart in the parking lot a close second. Everyone has a story, and in every story the dent happened to them. It's an old habit: when something goes wrong, the first thing the mind builds is an alibi. Katak falls roughly from mid-October to mid-November, the season when the crops that were sown come in. And Guru Arjan's Katak stanza opens with a line that takes the alibi apart.
screen: `A DENT THAT NOBODY MADE.` → `THE MIND BUILDS AN ALIBI.` → `KATAK: HARVEST SEASON.`

segments.voice: It begins katak karam kamaavane, dos na kaahoo jog. In paraphrase: in Katak, we earn what our deeds earn; no one else is to be blamed. Karam here is deeds, what you've actually done. Kamaavane is the everyday Punjabi word for earning, the way you earn wages. Dos is fault, blame. It's almost a farmer's line: what you planted is what's in the field, so there's no point shouting at the neighbor's crop. Then the stanza says where the trouble really starts. Forgetting the Lord, every illness takes hold. Turning your face away, you're separated, life after life. The world's pleasures turn bitter in an instant. So the deepest deed in the stanza isn't stealing or lying. It's forgetting. This isn't a stanza of doom. Sikh teaching holds deeds and grace together: you reap what you sow, and the Guru's mercy can still reach the field. And the stanza ends with the way out: in Katak, in the company of the holy, all worries fall away. Notice what owning a fault does. While you're busy blaming, you're stuck, because only the other person can fix it. The moment you say, that one was mine, you can apologize, repair, plant differently. Blaming no one isn't blaming yourself harshly. It's simply standing in your own field, honestly, and starting from there. Diwali, and with it the Sikh Bandi Chhor Divas, usually falls in this season of harvest: a festival of lamps for a month about seeing clearly.

segments.voice: Look back over the week for one small thing that went wrong where you'd been telling a story about someone else: a missed message, a sharp reply, a forgotten promise. Without punishing yourself, say inwardly, that part was mine, and notice how it feels to set the alibi down, and what small repair it opens. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Katak. In the Barah Maha, Katak is the honest month: we earn what our deeds earn, no one else is to blame, and the holy company lifts the worry.
Your line: katak: blame no one. Owning a fault is where mending starts. See you in Maghar.

574.title: The month of Maghar
574.hook: in Maghar lovely are those who sit with the Beloved (Barah Maha, ang 135)
574.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, Sikhs sit together on the floor of the diwan hall, at one level, to hear kirtan; on the Sangrand of Maghar gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza from the Barah Maha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katak: we earn what our deeds earn, and no one else is to blame. Today the week ends sitting down together.

Some good hours happen with nothing going on. A kitchen late at night, two people with tea, the dishes not done. A hospital waiting room where a friend just sits beside you and doesn't try to say anything wise. A grandparent on a bench, holding a small hand, watching pigeons. None of it would make a highlight reel, but these can be the moments that stay. Maghar, roughly mid-November to mid-December, is when the Punjabi cold comes in and people pull their chairs closer. Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza is about exactly that: sitting with.
screen: `TEA AT A LATE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `A FRIEND IN THE WAITING ROOM.` → `MAGHAR: SITTING WITH.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: in Maghar, lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, the Lord. Sohandee-aa, lovely, shining. Baithrree-aah, those who sit. That's all they're doing: not climbing, earning or proving, just seated beside the One they love, and the stanza says their beauty can't even be counted. Then the other side. Those who don't sit in the company of the holy stay alone. Their pain doesn't leave them, and they fall into death's grip. A whole Sikh practice lives inside that picture. In the diwan hall of a gurdwara, people take off their shoes, cover their heads, bow, and then sit on the floor, together, at the same level. Nobody has a better chair. They sit while the hymns are sung, sometimes a long time, sometimes saying nothing at all. That's sangat, the holy company, and in the Barah Maha it's where the bride finds the Beloved's presence. Look back over the week and you can see the road. In Jeth she bowed. In Asarh she learned to keep Him near in the heat. In Sawan she blossomed, in Bhadon she doubted, in Assu she longed and asked how, in Katak she stopped blaming. Now, in Maghar, she simply sits. The stanza ends: in Maghar, those who worship the Lord are not born again into the round of coming and going. The long journey of the months arrives somewhere very still.
screen: `SOHANDEE-AA: LOVELY ARE THOSE WHO SIT.` · `APART FROM THE HOLY, WE STAY ALONE.` · `SANGAT: SEATED ON ONE FLOOR.` · `THE WEEK'S ROAD ARRIVES IN STILLNESS.` · then, large: `MAGHAR: SIT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If someone you love is near, sit beside them now, no phone, no agenda; if not, bring one person to mind and sit as if they were next to you, their face, their hands, the way they settle into a chair. Don't plan a conversation; just be with. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the stanza calls the Beloved.
Maghar. In the Barah Maha, Maghar is the month of sitting: lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, and the holy company is where we sit.
Your line: maghar: sit together. Tea counts; a bench counts. Day five hundred seventy-four, done.
